Period schedule:

Total: 8 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Story Aloud: Seed to Sapling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.159): arrange story events in correct order.

time_bands.activity: Open the story to page 155. Invite students to look at the title and any illustrations, and share what they think the story will be about before reading begins.

Teacher reads Part I of the story aloud (pp.155–160) while students follow in their textbooks. Pause briefly at the moment Rakesh plants the seed and when the first shoot appears to allow a quick paired exchange on what they notice.
Using “Let us discuss” (p.159), students arrange the ten events in correct story order in pairs and then share with the class. Discuss the two events already placed as anchor points.

periods.teacher_notes: The story opens with Rakesh walking home eating cherries, and the grandfather’s prompt about luck drives the whole narrative forward — keep that exchange central during read-aloud. A common pitfall is treating the sequencing activity as a simple listing task; push students to justify each placement using details from the prose.

periods.activity_title: Causes, Effects and Close Reading of Extracts

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.164): complete cause-and-effect table for Part II.
Let us think and reflect (p.165): read Extract 1 and answer questions.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.165): read Extract 2 and answer all four questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Part II of the story aloud (pp.161–164) while students follow. Pause after each major setback — the goat, the scythe, the snow — for a quick verbal reaction from students.

Students complete the cause-and-effect table from “Let us discuss” (p.164) individually, then compare answers in pairs. Whole-class sharing follows, with the teacher drawing out rows 2, 3, and 4 where students often struggle.

Class works through Extract 1 from “Let us think and reflect” (p.165) together — the grandfather’s advice about luck and effort. Teacher facilitates discussion of the MCQ item on Rakesh’s mood and the short-answer item on the grandfather’s philosophy, inviting students to defend their choices with textual evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: Part II spans the tree’s repeated setbacks; students often focus only on the damage and miss the tree’s recovery as the thematic core — prompt them to find the line after each disaster where growth resumes. The grandfather’s remark ‘Nothing is lucky if you put it away’ is the moral hinge of the story and deserves sustained discussion.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.166): answer comprehension and inference questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Part III aloud (pp.165–172), covering the blossoms, the birds and insects, the full-grown tree, and Rakesh’s closing question. Students follow in their textbooks.

Students work individually on the factual and inferential questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.166) — covering why Rakesh’s parents sent him to Mussoorie, the praying-mantis episode, and life in the Himalayan foothills. Pairs compare answers before a whole-class check.

Whole-class discussion on the two extended-response questions: what Rakesh means by ‘Is this what it feels to be God?’ and what the story suggests about human–nature connections. Teacher invites varied interpretations and asks students to support each with a specific scene or line.

periods.teacher_notes: The closing question — ‘Is this what it feels to be God?’ — is the story’s most philosophically open moment; students need to connect it to the grandfather’s earlier remark about planting the tree themselves. Watch for responses that treat it only as pride in ownership rather than the deeper sense of nurturing and co-creation the narrative builds.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Environmental Heroes; Speaking in Syllables

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.170): identify four true statements from seven after the conversation.
Let us speak (p.167): read story words aloud, count syllables and check with classmates.

time_bands.activity: Briefly orient students to the listening task: they will hear a conversation about environmental movements and must identify four true statements from seven. Read the seven statements on page 170 together so students know what to listen for.

Teacher reads the conversation transcript aloud at a natural pace (p.201). Students listen and mark their choices. A second reading at a slower pace follows, after which pairs confer and agree on four true statements before whole-class verification.

Move to “Let us speak” (p.167). Students work in pairs: each partner reads the eleven words from the story aloud, writes the syllable count, then claps the beats to check. Pairs compare counts with neighbouring pairs and resolve any differences.
Two or three volunteers read each word aloud for the class with beats. Teacher confirms counts and models any word where syllable boundaries are uncertain (e.g., ‘Himalayan’, ‘caterpillar’).

periods.teacher_notes: The conversation covers the Chipko Movement, the Appiko Movement, Saalumarada Thimakka, and Jadav Payeng — students may confuse the movements, so a brief board-list of names after listening helps. In the syllable activity, multi-syllable words like ‘grandfather’ and ‘caterpillar’ commonly receive wrong counts; clapping with physical beats is more reliable than visual counting.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.168): prepare and deliver a short oral presentation on Van Mahotsav Diwas.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Van Mahotsav Diwas briefly — its name, timing, and connection to tree-planting. Students note down the five guiding points from “Let us speak” (p.168): when, who, why, how, and message. Pairs share any prior knowledge for two minutes.

Students prepare individually, writing three to four sentences for each guiding point in rough notes. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are unsure about ‘how it is celebrated’ to draw on the Chipko and Appiko conversations they heard.

Four to five volunteers deliver their oral presentations to the class (approximately two minutes each). After each, the class offers one appreciation and one suggestion. Teacher concludes with notes on confident pacing and how to connect a personal reason to the significance of the occasion.

periods.teacher_notes: Van Mahotsav Diwas is celebrated in the first week of July; students who are uncertain about content should be guided to connect it to the environmental values Ruskin Bond’s story raises. Students who hesitate to speak publicly benefit from hearing their peers first — volunteering order can be managed so less confident speakers go third or fourth.

periods.activity_title: Completing a Magazine Article: Trees—Our Lifeline

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.171–172): fill blanks (i)–(x) to complete the magazine article on trees.

time_bands.activity: Read the incomplete article on ‘Trees—Our Lifeline’ aloud together (pp.171–172), pausing at each blank so students can hear the flow. Identify the ten supplied words and phrases in the box and discuss what category each belongs to (title, connective, environmental term, conclusion).

Students complete blanks (i)–(x) individually. Teacher circulates, drawing attention to grammatical fit — whether a blank needs a noun phrase, a verb phrase, or a connective — and the logical sequence of the article’s paragraphs.

Whole-class sharing of answers for each blank in sequence. Where students differ (particularly blanks vii–viii, which involve conditional logic), teacher facilitates discussion of why one phrase fits better than another in context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently swap ‘If trees were not there’ and ‘our planet’ between blanks vii and viii because both fit thematically; draw attention to the sentence grammar around each blank to resolve the choice. The article’s structure — problem, function, conditional consequence, conclusion — mirrors the argumentative writing students will encounter in senior classes.

periods.activity_title: Word Families, Taste Words, Antonyms and Past Tenses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.166): identify the odd word in each of four sets.
Let us learn (p.167): match textual words with correct antonyms from the box.
Let us learn (p.167): underline verbs and identify tense forms in three story sentences.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.168): fill blanks (ii)–(x) with correct past-tense forms of bracketed verbs.

time_bands.activity: Students work through the four odd-word sets from “Let us learn” (p.166) individually, then compare in pairs. Whole-class discussion focuses on the criterion used for each set — manner of movement, texture, type of looking — rather than just the answer.

Students complete the antonyms task (p.167), choosing from the ten-word box to match eight textual words. Teacher draws attention to the two extra words in the box and asks students to explain why they are left over.

Teacher writes the three story sentences on the board and works through the tense identification task (p.167) with the class, underlining verbs and labelling Simple Past, Past Progressive, and Past Perfect. Students copy and then contrast the three forms through targeted questions — what was completed, what was ongoing, what was completed before another past event.

periods.teacher_notes: In the odd-word sets, students often misidentify the odd word in the ‘stared, peered, pecked, gazed’ group because ‘pecked’ looks like a visual verb — draw out that it describes a physical beak action, not a looking action. The Past Perfect in ‘Rakesh and Grandfather gazed at the tree as though it had performed a miracle’ is the most challenging of the three sentences; model it last after students are confident with the simpler forms.

periods.activity_title: Punctuation in Practice and Exploring Environmentalists

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.169): punctuate the unpunctuated paragraph about Roshni and her grandparents.
Let us explore (p.172): find information about an Indian environmentalist and share with classmates.

time_bands.activity: Students receive the unpunctuated paragraph about Roshni (p.169) and work individually to insert correct punctuation. After individual work, pairs exchange and discuss differences. Whole-class review on the board covers capital letters for names and sentence starts, commas in direct address, inverted commas for speech, and the apostrophe for possession.

Introduce the “Let us explore” task (p.172) about Indian environmentalists. Each student selects one environmentalist — from the story context, the listening conversation, or their own knowledge — and writes five key facts in rough notes within the available time.

Pairs share their chosen environmentalists with each other, then two or three volunteers present to the class. Teacher closes by connecting the work of real-world environmentalists to Rakesh’s small act of planting a single seed.

periods.teacher_notes: The unpunctuated paragraph is dense with direct speech, possessives, and proper nouns; students commonly miss the apostrophe in ‘grandparents’ house’ and the comma before a direct address. For the environmentalist research, students who draw on Jadav Payeng or Saalumarada Thimakka from the listening conversation will have a strong factual base to work from.

items.source_lo: Student reconstructs narrative sequence and identifies cause-effect relationships using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rakesh planting a cherry seed; seasonal setbacks; tree’s recovery; Ruskin Bond’s Himalayan foothills narrative.
items.item_stem: Which of the following correctly describes the order of events in the story of Rakesh and the cherry tree?

options.label: A
options.text: Rakesh planted the seed → the goat ate the leaves → the grass-cutter’s scythe cut the tree → the first blossom appeared.

options.label: B
options.text: The first blossom appeared → Rakesh planted the seed → the goat ate the leaves → the grass-cutter’s scythe cut the tree.

options.label: C
options.text: Rakesh planted the seed → the first blossom appeared → the goat ate the leaves → the grass-cutter’s scythe cut the tree.

options.label: D
options.text: The grass-cutter’s scythe cut the tree → Rakesh planted the seed → the goat ate the leaves → the first blossom appeared.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has reversed the planting and the blossom, perhaps recalling the blossom as the story’s opening image rather than its climax.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student places the blossom before the setbacks, missing that the setbacks (goat, scythe) precede the tree’s flowering.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has misread the narrative entirely, placing the grass-cutting episode before the seed is planted.

items.source_lo: Student reconstructs narrative sequence and identifies cause-effect relationships using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rakesh planting a cherry seed; seasonal setbacks; tree’s recovery; Ruskin Bond’s Himalayan foothills narrative.
items.item_stem: In the story, the cherry tree faces three serious threats — a goat, a grass-cutter’s scythe, and heavy winter snow. For each threat, identify what effect it had on the tree and what the tree did next. What does this pattern of damage and recovery suggest about the tree’s character as Ruskin Bond presents it?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The goat stripped all leaves; the scythe cut the trunk in two; the snow bent it low — yet after each event the tree sent out new shoots and continued growing. This repeated recovery presents the cherry tree as quietly resilient, mirroring Rakesh’s own steady growth and embodying the story’s theme that life persists through patient endurance.

items.source_lo: Student interprets character motivation and theme through critical reading of prose extracts.
items.source_context: Grandfather’s advice on luck and effort; Rakesh’s closing question ‘Is this what it feels to be God?’; human–nature bond.
items.item_stem: When Rakesh asks his grandfather whether cherry seeds are lucky and the grandfather replies, “Nothing is lucky if you put it away. If you want luck, you must put it to some use,” what does this exchange reveal about the grandfather’s belief about luck and human effort? Choose the best answer.

options.label: A
options.text: Luck is a fixed quality that some objects possess and others do not.

options.label: B
options.text: Luck only becomes meaningful when it is activated through deliberate action.

options.label: C
options.text: Cherry seeds have special powers that other seeds do not have.

options.label: D
options.text: Grandfather is warning Rakesh not to waste food.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has read the exchange literally, missing the grandfather’s philosophy that luck is dormant without effort.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has focused on the specific object (the seed) rather than the principle the grandfather is stating.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has interpreted the practical action of planting as a comment about waste rather than a lesson about effort and intention.

items.source_lo: Student interprets character motivation and theme through critical reading of prose extracts.
items.source_context: Grandfather’s advice on luck and effort; Rakesh’s closing question ‘Is this what it feels to be God?’; human–nature bond.
items.item_stem: At the end of the story, Rakesh whispers, “Is this what it feels to be God?” after touching the bark of the fully grown cherry tree. His grandfather has just said that the tree is special because ‘We planted it ourselves.’ Drawing on both moments, explain what Rakesh’s question suggests about the relationship between humans and nature as the story presents it. Your response should go beyond simply saying Rakesh is happy or proud.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Rakesh’s question suggests that the act of nurturing a living thing from a seed to a full-grown tree gives humans a sense of creative partnership with nature rather than mere ownership of it. The grandfather’s remark that ‘we planted it ourselves’ anchors the tree’s worth in the shared effort of caring, not in the tree’s size or beauty, and Rakesh’s whispered question extends that to a feeling of having participated in the act of creation itself.

items.source_lo: Student identifies accurate information and distinguishes true from false statements by listening critically to a spoken conversation.
items.source_context: Conversation about Chipko Movement, Appiko Movement, Saalumarada Thimakka, and Jadav Payeng’s forest.
items.item_stem: Read the following statements about the conversation between a son and his mother regarding environmental movements and activists. Mark each statement True or False.

options.text: The son says the Chipko Movement showed how common people can come together to make a difference.
The mother says the Appiko Movement replaced the Chipko Movement entirely.
The mother is curious to hear what the son’s teacher shared about Saalumarada Thimakka.
Jadav Payeng is described as having turned barren land into a forest by planting trees over thirty years.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — The son states: ‘It showed how people can also make a difference.’
2. False — The mother says the success of the Chipko Movement led to the Appiko Movement, not that one replaced the other.
3. True — The mother says: ‘I’m interested to know what your teacher has shared with you.’
4. True — The son confirms it took Jadav Payeng thirty years and he planted nearly forty million trees.

items.source_lo: Student identifies accurate information and distinguishes true from false statements by listening critically to a spoken conversation.
items.source_context: Conversation about Chipko Movement, Appiko Movement, Saalumarada Thimakka, and Jadav Payeng’s forest.
items.item_stem: In the conversation, the son describes what he admires about Saalumarada Thimakka and what inspired him about Jadav Payeng. In two to three sentences, explain what each of these two environmentalists is known for, according to the conversation, and identify one quality or achievement the son specifically expresses admiration for.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Saalumarada Thimakka is an Indian environmentalist who has been planting trees since 1948 and has planted over 8,000 trees near her village; the son admires her commitment to conserving the environment. Jadav Payeng single-handedly turned approximately one thousand acres of barren land into a lush green forest by planting nearly forty million trees over thirty years; the son found him inspiring after reading a book and watching a documentary about him.

items.item_stem: Read aloud the following four words from the story — ‘grandfather’, ‘caterpillar’, ‘Himalayan’, and ‘disturbed’ — clapping once for each syllable as you say each word. Then state the number of syllables in each word and explain to a partner how you identified where one syllable ends and the next begins in ‘Himalayan’.

expected_elements: Correctly produces: grandfather (3), caterpillar (4), Himalayan (4), disturbed (2).
Claps in time with spoken syllables, not letter count.
Explains the syllable break in Himalayan: Hi-ma-la-yan.
Speaks clearly enough for the partner to hear and verify each beat.

items.source_context: Syllable counting with story words; oral presentation on Van Mahotsav Diwas and its environmental significance.
items.item_stem: Deliver a short oral presentation on Van Mahotsav Diwas to your class. Your presentation should address when the occasion is observed, who participates, why it is significant, how it is typically celebrated, and what message it carries for young people. Connect the significance of Van Mahotsav Diwas to the act of planting and nurturing trees as the story of Rakesh and the cherry tree illustrates.

expected_elements: States when Van Mahotsav Diwas is observed and who participates.
Gives at least one reason for its significance and one way it is celebrated.
Makes a clear connection to the story’s theme of nurturing a living thing.
Speaks in an organised sequence and maintains eye contact with the audience.

items.source_lo: Student completes a functional article by selecting contextually appropriate words and phrases to build a coherent argument.
items.source_context: Magazine article ‘Trees—Our Lifeline’: environmental functions of trees, conditional consequences of deforestation.
items.item_stem:
Below is the opening of a short magazine article about trees. Fill in the blanks using the words and phrases from the box provided. Box: absorb carbon dioxide, reduces pollution, would stop existing, ensures a better future, climate control, Moreover, If trees were not there, our planet, To conclude.

Trees — Our Lifeline

Trees are the lungs of our planet. Without them, life as we know it (i) ________________. They (ii) ________________ and release oxygen, helping us breathe. This process also (iii) ________________ and keeps the environment clean. (iv) ________________, trees give us fruits, nuts, and other foods, and they help in (v) ________________ and prevention of soil erosion. (vi) ________________, the air would be polluted, and we would struggle to breathe. (vii) ________________ would be barren, lacking food, shelter, and life-giving greenery. (viii) ________________, trees are true friends, and protecting and planting them (ix) ________________ for everyone on Earth.

expected_elements: Selects contextually correct phrase for each blank without substitution.
Maintains grammatical fit between the blank and its surrounding sentence.
Preserves the article’s logical flow: function → conditional consequence → conclusion.
Uses each word or phrase from the box exactly once, leaving none unused or repeated.

items.source_lo: Student completes a functional article by selecting contextually appropriate words and phrases to build a coherent argument.
items.source_context: Magazine article ‘Trees—Our Lifeline’: environmental functions of trees, conditional consequences of deforestation.
items.item_stem: Write a short opinion paragraph of five to seven sentences for a school magazine on the topic: ‘Planting a single tree can make a difference.’ Draw on the environmental roles of trees (such as absorbing carbon dioxide, preventing soil erosion, providing habitat) and use at least one example from real life or from a story or event you know to support your view. Use appropriate connectives such as ‘Moreover’, ‘Additionally’, and ‘To conclude’ to link your ideas.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion in the opening sentence.
Mentions at least two environmental functions of trees with accurate vocabulary.
Includes a specific real-life or textual example to support the argument.
Uses at least two connectives correctly to sequence ideas.

items.source_context: Odd-word sets from story vocabulary; antonyms for textual words including tender, sturdy, warmth, grumpy, sheltered.
items.item_stem: In the story, Ruskin Bond uses precise verbs to describe how characters and creatures move and look. Consider the group of four words: ‘stared, peered, pecked, gazed.’ Three of these words describe a way of looking. Identify the odd word out, explain in one sentence why it does not belong with the others, and then use the odd word correctly in a sentence of your own about the cherry tree or a bird that visits it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: ‘Pecked’ is the odd word out because it describes a physical action performed with a beak, not a way of directing one’s eyes. An acceptable original sentence: ‘A bulbul pecked at the small red cherries hanging from the lower branches.’

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies past tense forms in context, including Simple Past, Past Progressive, and Past Perfect.
items.source_context: Tense identification in story sentences; punctuation of a narrative paragraph involving direct speech, apostrophes, and proper nouns.
items.item_stem:
Read the following three sentences from the story and identify the tense form of each underlined verb phrase. Write your answers as: sentence number — tense form — one-sentence reason.

1. Rakesh (was on his way) home from school when he (bought) the cherries.
2. Rakesh (was looking) for Grandfather without finding him.
3. Rakesh and Grandfather (gazed) at the tree as though it (had performed) a miracle.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. ‘was on his way’ — Past Progressive — it describes an action in progress at the moment he bought the cherries; ‘bought’ — Simple Past — a completed action at a specific point in the past. 2. ‘was looking’ — Past Progressive — an ongoing search at that moment. 3. ‘gazed’ — Simple Past — a completed action; ‘had performed’ — Past Perfect — the miracle was completed before the gazing occurred.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies past tense forms in context, including Simple Past, Past Progressive, and Past Perfect.
items.source_context: Tense identification in story sentences; punctuation of a narrative paragraph involving direct speech, apostrophes, and proper nouns.
items.item_stem: Write a short paragraph of four to five sentences describing a moment in Rakesh’s life from the story — such as the evening he found the first small shoot, or the February morning his grandfather spotted the first blossom. Use at least one example each of Simple Past tense, Past Progressive tense, and Past Perfect tense in your paragraph. Underline each tense form and label it in brackets.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any four-to-five sentence paragraph drawn from the story’s events that correctly deploys and labels all three tense forms. The Simple Past should describe a completed action, the Past Progressive an ongoing one, and the Past Perfect an action completed before another past action. Verify that the underlined forms match their labels and that the paragraph is grounded in the story’s content.

items.item_stem: Jadav Payeng of Assam and Saalumarada Thimakka of Karnataka are two Indian environmentalists known for their extraordinary commitment to planting and protecting trees. Choose one of them. Write five key facts about their life and conservation work, and explain in two to three sentences why their work matters for the environment today.

expected_elements: States five accurate facts about the chosen environmentalist’s life and work.
Connects their work to a specific environmental benefit such as habitat creation or pollution reduction.
Uses formal written English with complete sentences.
Shows understanding that individual effort can produce large-scale environmental change.

items.source_lo: Student researches and presents information about real-world environmental conservationists using project-work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Indian environmentalists including Jadav Payeng, Saalumarada Thimakka, Kailash Sankhala; project on conservation work.
items.item_stem: Create a one-page informational profile of an Indian environmentalist of your choice — someone not already covered in your textbook discussion. Your profile should include: the person’s name and region, the environmental problem they addressed, the actions they took, the impact of their work, and why you chose them. Present your profile to your class in three to four minutes, using your notes as a guide rather than reading word for word.

expected_elements: Profile covers all five required elements: name and region, problem, actions, impact, personal reason.
Information is accurate and drawn from a reliable source.
Presentation uses notes rather than reading directly from the page.
Student makes a clear connection between the individual’s work and broader environmental benefit.
